read.sections.0.heading.source: From rules to learning from text
read.sections.0.heading.back: From rules to learning from text

read.sections.0.text.source: A chatbot is a computer program that you can chat with in writing. Chatbots are not new. In 1966, a program called ELIZA chatted by following rules that people wrote. Today, many chatbots are built on a large language model, or LLM, which uses machine learning instead. An LLM learns patterns from a huge amount of text, such as books, articles and web pages, much of it written by people. LLMs grew from the same things as the photo programs in Lesson 2: lots of digital data and fast chips. In 2017, researchers published a new design for language tasks, and many later LLMs were built on it. In November 2022, the company OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot built on an LLM.
read.sections.0.text.back: A chatbot is a computer program you can talk to by writing. Chatbots are not new. In 1966 a program called ELIZA talked with people by following rules people wrote. Today many chatbots are built on a large language model, or LLM, which uses machine learning instead. A model like this learns patterns from huge amounts of text, such as books, articles and web pages, much of which was written by people. Large language models grew from the same things as the picture program in Lesson 2: lots of digital data and fast chips. In 2017 researchers published a new design for language tasks, and many later large language models were built on this design. In November 2022 the company OpenAI launched ChatGPT, a chatbot built on a large language model.
read.sections.0.text.note: Reviewer: “much of it written by people”: ส่วนใหญ่ (most) changed to จำนวนมาก (much); the English avoids saying most on purpose (educatorNotes.0).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: A chatbot is a program you can chat with. In 1966, a chatbot called ELIZA followed rules that people wrote. Many chatbots now use a large language model, or LLM. An LLM learns from lots of text instead, like books and web pages. People wrote much of it. Like the photo programs in Lesson 2, LLMs needed lots of data and fast chips. In 2017, researchers made a new design. Many later LLMs used it. ChatGPT, built on an LLM, came out in 2022.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A chatbot is a program you can talk to. In 1966 a chatbot called ELIZA followed rules people wrote. Today many chatbots use a large language model. This kind of model learns from lots of text instead, such as books and web pages. Much of the text was written by people. Like the picture program in Lesson 2, this model needs lots of data and fast chips. In 2017 researchers thought up a new design. Many later models used this design. In 2022 ChatGPT came out. It is a chatbot that uses a large language model.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How it writes, one piece at a time
read.sections.1.heading.back: How it writes, one piece at a time

read.sections.1.text.source: An LLM works with small pieces of text called tokens. A token may be a word or part of a word. Suppose a learner asks, “What is a map scale?” The model predicts a likely first token, such as “A”. It adds it, then predicts the next one, such as “map”, using everything written so far. It goes on, piece by piece, until the answer is finished. A toy example shows the idea. In the Lakeside word game, “tea” came after “a cup of” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once. Real models do not just count words; they learn far richer patterns from far more text. Often each token is picked partly by chance from the likely ones, so the same question can get different answers. With other settings, a model can give the same answer every time.
read.sections.1.text.back: A large language model works with small pieces of text called tokens. A token may be one word or part of a word. Suppose a learner asks “What is a map's scale (มาตราส่วน)?” The model predicts a likely first token, such as “มาตรา”. It adds that token, then predicts the next token, such as “ส่วน”, by looking at everything written so far. It goes on like this, one piece at a time, until the answer is finished. A model example helps you picture it. In Lakeside's word game, the word “tea” follows “in the cup there is” six times, “water” three times and “rice” once. A real model does not just count words; it learns much more complex patterns from much more text. Often each token is chosen partly by chance from the likely ones, so the same question can get different answers. But with other settings, the model can give the same answer every time.
read.sections.1.text.note: Token example: the English answer starts “A” then “map”. In Thai the answer starts “มาตราส่วน...”, so the tokens are “มาตรา” then “ส่วน”, which also shows a token being part of a word. Also in glossary examples 2 and 3. Check this split sounds right to a reader who knows how Thai is tokenised.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Why it matters for writing, translation and information
read.sections.2.heading.back: Why this matters for writing, translating and information

read.sections.2.text.source: LLMs are now used to help people write, translate and look for information. A chatbot can explain an idea in simpler words, help with a first draft or translate a short notice. At Lakeside, a teacher checked the helper's explanation, and it was right. A volunteer fixed two words in its translation. Many LLMs learned mainly from English, and researchers have found they usually work worse in languages with little writing online. A basic LLM predicts words that sound right; nothing in that checks the facts. So it can make things up and still sound confident, like the Lakeside helper that named a book that does not exist. Some tools also search the web and show links, but the pages can be wrong or misread. Check important answers with a trusted source, such as a library or a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.back: Today large language models are used to help people write, translate and find information. A chatbot can explain an idea in simpler words, help draft a first version, or translate a short notice. At Lakeside a teacher checked the assistant's explanation, and it was correct. A volunteer fixed two words in its translation. Many large language models learned mainly from English, and researchers found they often work worse in languages with little writing online. A base model predicts words that sound right, but no part of that process checks facts. So it can make things up and still sound confident, like the Lakeside assistant naming a book that does not exist. Some tools search the web and show links too, but those pages may be wrong or misread. Check important answers against a reliable source, such as a library or a teacher.

watch.summary.source: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from a huge amount of text from the internet. The main idea is simple. It uses numbers about what is likely, worked out very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by the writer Shakespeare. It counts which letter often comes after each letter. When it writes this way, the words look strange. When it looks at longer pieces, like whole words, its guesses get much better. Big models use neural networks, which are loosely based on the brain. People also helped to make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.
watch.summary.back: In this video, two people who build AI tools explain how chatbots work. One works at the company that made ChatGPT. A large language model learns from huge amounts of text from the internet. The main idea is simple: it uses numbers that say what is likely to happen, which can be calculated very fast. The video shows a small example. A program reads plays by a writer named Shakespeare. It counts which letters usually follow each letter. When it writes this way, the words look odd. But when it looks at longer pieces, such as whole words, its guesses get much better. Large models use neural networks, which take a rough idea from the brain. People also help make ChatGPT's answers better. But its answers still come from what is likely, so it can make mistakes.

educatorNotes.0.source: There is no real chatbot in the app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). The Lakeside word game, the helper's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are made up. The cup-of-tea game is a toy analogy, not how real models work: real LLMs learn far richer patterns over tokens from far more text, and keep no table of counts. Not all training text is written by people (some models also learn from computer-made text), so the lesson says “much of it”. A model can repeat an answer: an app can pick the likeliest token every time, or pick at random among likely ones (Google's course).
educatorNotes.0.back: There is no real chatbot in the app (docs/content/DIGITAL_WORLD_SPEC.md 5.6). Lakeside's word game, the assistant's answers and the book “The Long Blue Road” are fictional. The “in the cup there is” word game is a simple comparison, not how real models work. Real large language models learn much more complex token patterns from much more text, and do not keep a table of counts. The training text was not all written by people (some models learn from computer-made text too), so the lesson says “much”. A model can repeat the same answer because the app may pick the most likely token every time, or sample from the likely ones (Google's course). In the Thai version the word game uses “ในถ้วยมี” instead of the English “a cup of”, and the token example is “มาตรา” and “ส่วน” instead of “A” and “map”.

educatorNotes.1.source: A basic model writes from what it learned; some tools also search the web or a set of documents and show links. A link is not proof: open it and check it, as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT, “How do I fact-check AI search results?”, 2025). The history thread: ELIZA (1966) chatted by rules people wrote; LLMs use machine learning, which grew with digital text and fast chips, as in Lesson 2; the 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani and others), which Google's Machine Learning Crash Course calls “the most successful and widely used architecture for building LLMs”. Lesson 7 goes further into which languages these tools serve well.
educatorNotes.1.back: A base model writes from what it has learned. Some tools also search the web or a set of documents and show links. Links are not evidence: open and check them as in Lesson 14 (Stanford CRAFT, “How do I fact-check AI search results?”, 2025). The history thread: ELIZA (1966) talked using rules people wrote, while large language models use machine learning, which grew along with digital text and fast chips, as in Lesson 2. The 2017 design is the transformer (Vaswani et al.), which Google's Machine Learning Crash Course calls “the most successful and widely used architecture for building large language models”. Lesson 7 goes deeper into which languages these tools work well in.
